## Chapter Summary

A relational database stores each fact once and links its tables through keys, so most accounting questions require joining tables. An inner join returns the pairs of rows whose keys match, and table aliases keep a join readable and resolve column names that appear in both tables. Because the Charles River database declares no foreign keys, every join is tested by comparing the number of rows it returns with the number it should return. A left join keeps every row of the first table, with NULLs where the second table has no match. It lists a whole population, and, written as an anti-join, it finds the records that have no match at all. A condition on the second table belongs in the ON clause, because in WHERE it turns the left join into an inner join.

Aggregate functions calculate one value from many rows. COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX skip NULLs, except `COUNT(*)`, which counts rows. GROUP BY calculates them once per group, and every column of the SELECT list must either be grouped or aggregated, even though SQLite does not insist on it. Grouping by the key rather than the name keeps records that share a name apart. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, while WHERE filters rows before it. A join from a header to its lines repeats the header's amounts on every line, so each amount must be summed at the level of the table it belongs to. Subqueries answer questions in two steps: in WHERE they supply a value or a list, and in FROM they form derived tables that can be summarized first and joined afterward. A query is evaluated in the order FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, and LIMIT, which explains where each kind of condition belongs.

Applied to the controller's questions, the queries showed that the manufacturing variance of fiscal 2026 ties to the ledger to the cent, and that it rose from year to year across the item groups the plant makes, with Furniture carrying most of it. The same joins rebuilt the pre-closing trial balance of fiscal 2026 and followed the conversion cost through account 1090 Manufacturing Cost Clearing, where the payroll charged to production rose while the standard cost released by completions stayed nearly flat. Output did not fall. The manufacturing payroll paid the same number of people for more hours each year, with overtime more than doubling, so the paid hours per standard hour of output rose to about one and a half. The variance measures the cost of those extra hours.
